subject: Japan hiked to 1.25% and Canadian yields followed
bodyMarkdown:
If you renew a mortgage in the next year, Friday's decision in Tokyo is already sitting in the quote you are going to get. Canada's five-year bond yield finished the week at 3.60%, and lenders have been repricing fixed mortgages all month.

## What the Bank of Japan did on Friday

The Bank of Japan raised its policy rate by a quarter point to 1.25% on Friday, the highest it has been in 31 years, CNBC reported the same day. The board split 7 to 2, with two members voting to hold, and the new rate takes effect on September 24. Then came the odd part. The yen fell instead of rising, sliding past 157 per dollar, because the two dissents and Governor Kazuo Ueda's refusal to promise anything further told traders the tightening may stop here. Bloomberg reported Friday that Ueda is working between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has been pressing Japan to tighten faster, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who wants growth. It was Ueda's second hike in three months.

## Why a Tokyo rate sets a price in Toronto

Japanese pension funds and insurers are among the largest foreign owners of government bonds anywhere, and for three decades they bought abroad because home paid close to nothing. That reason is gone. Nikkei Asia reported that Japan's 10-year government bond yield briefly touched 3% in early September, a three-decade high, as part of a global selloff in sovereign debt, and the 30-year hit a record 3.28% on September 3. Bloomberg wrote on September 8 that money managers were arguing over **repatriation risk**, the chance that Japanese investors sell their foreign bonds and bring the money home, and that markets were underpricing how quickly that could happen. Canada sits on the receiving end. Our five-year yield rose to 3.60% on September 18, roughly a quarter point higher over the week, and Canadian Mortgage Trends reported that lenders answered by raising fixed rates, by 20 basis points at some and close to 100 at others.

## The Bank of Canada is not driving this

The Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at 2.25% on September 2, and its next decision lands October 28 with the quarterly Monetary Policy Report. That overnight rate steers variable mortgages. Fixed mortgages are priced off the **five-year Government of Canada bond yield**, the market's cost of lending to Ottawa for five years, plus a lender spread of about one to two points. So Tiff Macklem can sit perfectly still while your renewal quote climbs, which is roughly what August and September have looked like. The Fed added to it. CNBC reported that on September 16 it lifted its target range to 3.75% to 4%, a first hike since 2023 on a 12 to 0 vote, and that 16 of 18 officials saw room for another this year. Canadian inflation ran 3.0% in August, Statistics Canada said on September 14, with gasoline up 22.8% from a year earlier.

## The takeaway

Ratehub listed the best five-year fixed at 4.09% this week, and if you renew before next summer, call your lender on Monday and ask for a rate hold. Follow the five-year Government of Canada yield daily on the Bank of Canada's own rates page rather than waiting on the October 28 announcement, because the bond is what your lender is watching. Keep an eye on the yen as well, since a move back toward 150 would say traders expect more hikes from Ueda, and that gives Japanese money another reason to leave foreign bonds. I could be wrong on direction, and one weak Canadian jobs report would pull the five-year back down quickly.
